notes: REAL PRIMARY DATA from two official OECD sources, combined into one file: (1) MANDATORY PENSION CONTRIBUTION RATES for an average worker in 2022 (latest available), from Table 8.1 of the OECD's biennial 'Pensions at a Glance 2023: OECD and G20 Indicators' report (PDF: https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/12/pensions-at-a-glance-2023_4757bf20/678055dd-en.pdf). Figures cover contributions to MANDATORY AND QUASI-MANDATORY pension schemes (public plus, where applicable, mandatory/auto-enrolment private/occupational schemes), split into employee/employer and public/private components, plus an 'effective rate on average earnings' that accounts for contribution ceilings. (2) PENSION REPLACEMENT RATES for 2024 (gross and net, at 100% of average wage, mandatory schemes only, combining public and private mandatory pensions), fetched directly from the OECD's live SDMX data API (dataflow OECD.ELS.SPD:DSD_PAG@DF_PRR, measures GPRR100/NPRR100, optionality=Mandatory) which underlies the 'Pensions at a Glance' indicator pages e.g. https://www.oecd.org/en/data/indicators/net-pension-replacement-rates.html and https://www.oecd.org/en/data/indicators/gross-pension-replacement-rates.html. Values were identical for Male and Female in the fetched data for all 8 target countries at the 100%-of-average-wage income level (differences by sex mainly arise at other earnings levels or in countries with sex-specific retirement ages/rules not reflected in this file). VINTAGE MISMATCH CAVEAT: contribution rates are for 2022 (Table 8.1, the latest published in the 2023 biennial report; the next edition, 'Pensions at a Glance 2025', was not yet available as a machine-readable table at the time of this pull) while replacement rates are the 2024 vintage from the live data API -- these two vintages are combined in a single row per country for convenience but are NOT from the same survey year; treat contribution-rate figures as materially unchanged since 2022 unless a specific country is known to have reformed its pension system since then. CATEGORY MAPPING / DEFINITIONS: 'pension_contribution_effective_rate_avg_earnings_pct' is the headline summary figure most useful for the v2 discretionary-income calculation (it already nets out the effect of contribution ceilings and, in Finland's/Switzerland's case, age-varying rates); 'nominal_total' is the simple sum of nominal employee+employer public+private rates before applying any ceiling and can exceed the effective rate for countries with earnings ceilings (e.g. Switzerland: nominal 21.2% vs effective 17.3%). UK figures are notably broader than pure old-age pension contributions -- OECD Table 8.1 notes UK's reported rate 'covers old age, survivor, disability, sickness and maternity, work injury, and unemployment' (i.e. it is essentially the full UK National Insurance rate, not an isolated pension contribution) -- treat the UK figure as an upper-bound proxy for pension-specific burden. Sweden and Norway's 'private' components include mandatory occupational/auto-enrolment schemes (not voluntary savings) so they belong in a 'mandatory pension contribution' bucket, not the v2 schema's 'voluntary_savings' category. 'gross_replacement_rate' = pension benefit as % of gross pre-retirement earnings at the average-wage level; 'net_replacement_rate' = pension entitlement as % of NET (after-tax) pre-retirement earnings, both for MANDATORY schemes only (public + mandatory private/occupational), excluding voluntary private pensions -- net rates are systematically higher than gross rates because retirees typically face lower effective tax and social-contribution rates than workers. USAGE NOTE FOR v2 FRONTEND: this file is country-level (not by-decile/household-type) and is intended to provide (a) a standard mandatory-pension-contribution-rate deduction to subtract from gross income before computing discretionary income for each non-US country (the US-specific equivalent, Social Security's 6.2% employee OASDI + Medicare 1.45% FICA, is already implicit in the BLS CES after-tax income figures and should NOT be double-counted using this file's US row), and (b) a reference replacement-rate figure for any future 'retirement adequacy' feature. All 8 target countries plus the OECD-35 average are included.
